chief_complaint: midline painless neck lump that moves upward when swallowing
hpi_details: A 74-year-old female presents to the clinic with midline painless neck lump that moves upward when swallowing. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks it is an enlarged thyroid gland or a swollen lymph node caused by feeling run down recently.
concerns: She is worried the lump could be a malignant throat or thyroid tumor like the one a close friend had.
expectations: She hopes to get an ultrasound or neck scan today to find out exactly what the lump is.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Thyroglossal Duct Cyst evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Thyroglossal Duct Cyst is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
A new adult midline neck mass warrants ultrasound assessment of the lesion and thyroid, with specialist evaluation and tissue sampling of suspicious findings before proceeding to definitive surgery.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Thyroglossal Duct Cyst.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Dermoid cyst without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Rapid growth or hardness — rare malignant transformation should be excluded.
management_principles: Obtain neck and thyroid ultrasound; arrange specialist evaluation and sample suspicious adult neck-mass findings before definitive surgery
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: midline painless neck lump that moves upward when swallowing

A 74-year-old female presents to the clinic with midline painless neck lump that moves upward when swallowing. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Thyroglossal Duct Cyst.
reference_soap.assessment: Presentation consistent with a Thyroglossal Duct Cyst: painless midline neck mass that elevates with swallowing; given the patient's age, malignancy must be excluded before proceeding to definitive surgery.
reference_soap.plan: Obtain neck and thyroid ultrasound and arrange prompt ENT evaluation. In this older adult, assess for malignancy and obtain needle sampling of suspicious lesions or lymph nodes before planning a Sistrunk procedure.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Thyroglossal Duct Cyst
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Thyroglossal Duct Cyst
Implement evidence-based management plan: adult neck-mass evaluation before definitive Sistrunk surgery

teaching.one_liner: A congenital cyst from an incompletely closed thyroid developmental tract, presenting as a midline neck lump that characteristically moves upward with swallowing.
red_flags: Rapid growth or hardness — rare malignant transformation should be excluded

must_ask.say: Does the lump move up when you swallow?
Is it exactly in the middle of your neck?
Is it painful, or has it ever been infected?
How long have you had this?

history.answer: I noticed a lump right in the middle of my neck recently, and it moves upward whenever I swallow.
I first discovered it about three weeks ago while washing my face.
It seems to have enlarged slightly over the past few weeks, but it did not balloon up overnight.
It is positioned directly in the center of my neck, just above my Adam's apple area.
No, it doesn't cause any pain, and it does not hurt even when I press on it.
Yes, it moves up noticeably whenever I swallow water or stick my tongue out.
No, eating meals doesn't change its size at all, and I have no pain while chewing or eating.
No, I have checked my collarbone, underarms, and groin, and there are no lumps anywhere else.
I have been feeling quite worn out and fatigued over the past couple of weeks.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or sweating episodes.
No, my weight has stayed stable, and I do not wake up drenched in sweat.
No, I have not had a sore throat, cough, toothache, or any skin infections recently.
No, food and liquids go down without trouble, and I have no shortness of breath.
No, my voice sounds completely normal and hasn't become raspy.
No, I don't have earaches, a blocked nose, or nosebleeds.
No, I haven't had racing heartbeats, hand tremors, or trouble handling heat or cold.
No, I have never had radiation treatments to my head, neck, or chest.
No, I have never had tuberculosis, and I haven't been in contact with anyone who had it.
No, I don't keep any pets and have not been bitten or scratched by cats or other animals.
I read an article about something called a thyroglossal cyst, and I wondered if it could be that.
I'm worried sick that this lump could be cancer, especially since a good friend of mine had a neck growth that turned out malignant.
I'm hoping to get an ultrasound or scan done today so we can see what's actually sitting in the middle of my neck.
I have been generally healthy and don't have high blood pressure, diabetes, or any other long-term illnesses.
I have never had any surgeries or been admitted to a hospital.
I am not taking any prescription drugs, over-the-counter medicines, or dietary supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or anything else.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I only have about half a glass of wine once or twice a month on social occasions.
I am a retired teacher and live comfortably at home with my husband.
No one in my family has had thyroid cancer, neck tumors, or any other serious neck conditions.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 124/76 mmHg, heart rate is 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 98% on room air, and body temperature is 36.6 degrees Celsius.
An alert elderly female in no acute distress with a visible midline swelling in the anterior neck.
A 2.5 cm smooth, round, non-tender, mobile cystic mass is palpated in the midline neck over the thyrohyoid region; no cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy is noted.
The anterior midline neck mass clearly elevates with deglutition and tongue protrusion; the thyroid gland is normal in size and consistency with no nodules or goiter.
The oral mucosa, tongue base, tonsils, and pharynx appear clear without mucosal ulceration, masses, or pooling of secretions.
Both tympanic membranes are intact, translucent, and free of effusion or erythema.
Skin over the anterior neck mass is intact without erythema, punctum, fistulous tract, or discharge.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally on auscultation with no stridor, wheezing, or crackles.
Regular rhythm with normal heart sounds S1 and S2; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops heard.
